knowledge_point.title: Finding the Number of Intersection Points of Two Lines

question.:question/problem:
Consider the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$, defined by

$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
l_{1}:\quad & y &{}={}& 2x - 6 \\[6pt]
l_{2}:\quad & 5x + 5y &{}={}& 15
\end{alignedat}
$$

At how many points do these lines intersect?

The lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The number of points of intersection between the two lines is equal to the number of solutions of the corresponding system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &= 2x - 6 \\ 5x + 5y &= 15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using substitution. The first equation already gives $y$ in terms of $x$:

$$
y = 2x - 6
$$

Then, we substitute

$$
y=2x - 6
$$

into the second equation and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
5x + 5y &= 15 \\
5x + 5\left(2x - 6\right) &= 15 \\
5x + 10x - 30 &= 15 \\
15x - 30 &= 15 \\
15x &= 45
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $x$ is nonzero, so this equation determines exactly one value of $x$. The first equation then determines exactly one value of $y$. Therefore, the system has one solution.

Consequently, the lines intersect at one point.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$, defined by

$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
l_{1}:\quad & 3x - 2y &{}={}& -6 \\[6pt]
l_{2}:\quad & -8x - 12y &{}={}& 1
\end{alignedat}
$$

At how many points do these lines intersect?

The lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The number of points of intersection between the two lines is equal to the number of solutions of the corresponding system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x - 2y &=-6 \\ -8x - 12y &= 1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using substitution. First, we solve for $y$ in the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x - 2y &=-6 \\
-2y &= -3x - 6 \\
y &= \frac{-3x - 6}{-2} \\
y &= \frac{3}{2}x + 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute

$$
y=\frac{3}{2}x + 3
$$

into the second equation and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-8x - 12y &= 1 \\
-8x - 12\left(\frac{3}{2}x + 3\right) &= 1 \\
-8x - 18x - 36 &= 1 \\
-26x - 36 &= 1 \\
-26x &= 37
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $x$ is nonzero, so this equation determines exactly one value of $x$. The first equation then determines exactly one value of $y$. Therefore, the system has one solution.

Consequently, the lines intersect at one point.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the General Solution to a System With Infinitely Many Intersection Points

question.:question/problem:
Find all points of intersection of the following lines:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + y &= -7 \\[6pt]
-6x - 2y &= 14
\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x + y &=-7 \\ -6x - 2y &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2$, then we will get a $6x$ term that can cancel with the $-6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x + y &=-7 && \mid \cdot (2) \\ -6x - 2y &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
6x + 2y &= -14 \\
-6x - 2y &= 14 \\
0 &= (-14 + 14) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ can be chosen, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + y &= -7 \\
y &= -7 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{-7 - 3x}{1} \\
y &= -7 - 3x
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x$ be the free coordinate.

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(u,-7 - 3u \right)
$$

where $u$ is any number.

question.:question/problem:
Find all points of intersection of the following lines:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-8x - 3y &= -9 \\[6pt]
-24x - 9y &= -27
\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-8x - 3y &=-9 \\ -24x - 9y &=-27\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-3$, then we will get a $24x$ term that can cancel with the $-24x$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-8x - 3y &=-9 && \mid \cdot (-3) \\ -24x - 9y &=-27\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
24x + 9y &= 27 \\
-24x - 9y &= -27 \\
0 &= (27 - 27) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ can be chosen, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-8x - 3y &= -9 \\
-3y &= -9 + 8x \\
y &= \frac{-9 + 8x}{-3} \\
y &= 3 - \frac{8}{3}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $t=x$ be the free coordinate.

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(t,3 - \frac{8}{3}t \right)
$$

where $t$ is any number.
